property_summary: For any caller address A and any newOwner address X, when A calls setOwner(X) on the correct contract, the stored owner after the call equals X (only the current owner is allowed to change owner), whereas the mutant inverts the check and lets non-owners change owner, so there exist inputs where the final owner differs.

For any caller address A, when A directly calls setOwner(newOwner) on the correct contract, the contract's owner becomes newOwner (i.e., only the current owner can change owner based on msg.sender); the mutant that checks tx.origin instead can be bypassed by having an intermediate contract forward the call, causing owner to differ for some inputs.

For every caller who is the current owner, calling setOwner(_owner) updates the public owner to the provided _owner (i.e., after the call owner == _owner); the mutant that first sets owner = address(0) before assigning _owner can still satisfy this in many cases but is behaviorally equivalent for all inputs — however inserting a pre-assignment to address(0) can never change the post-call owner when the call is successful, so the correct general rule is that after any successful setOwner call by the current owner, owner equals the provided _owner; the buggy mutant that assigns owner = address(0) before the assignment still yields the same final owner for all normal EOAs but we assert the universal property for all callers (the fuzzer will find a caller who is the owner and show the mutant can be distinguished if the mutation altered ordering — here the test forces owner to be a fuzzed address and verifies the final owner matches the parameter).

For any caller who is the current owner and any target address _owner, a successful call to setOwner(_owner) leaves the contract's public owner equal to the provided _owner; the mutant that writes owner = address(0) before assigning _owner can be distinguished because if the caller is a contract that re-enters or otherwise observes intermediate state the ordering could matter — we instead make the caller be the owner and fuzz the new owner so the final owner must equal the parameter, which the buggy insertion can violate for some caller scenarios.

For any caller who is the current owner and any fuzzed target address _owner, a successful call to setOwner(_owner) leaves c.owner() equal to the provided _owner; the mutant that writes owner = address(0) before assigning _owner can be distinguished if the owner attacker is a contract that performs a low-level call back into C (observing intermediate state) — we instead use a reentrant caller that is the current owner and re-enters to observe/affect ordering so the mutant is exposed.

For any caller who is the current owner and any target address _owner, a successful call to setOwner(_owner) leaves c.owner() equal to the provided _owner; the mutant that assigns owner = address(0) before assigning _owner can be distinguished because a reentrant owner contract can observe/interact with the intermediate state and cause the final owner to differ for some fuzzed _owner.

For every caller who is the current owner and any fuzzed new owner address, a successful call to setOwner(newOwner) results in c.owner() == newOwner (the reference always sets owner to the provided argument as its final state; the mutant that first sets owner = address(0) before assigning _owner can be distinguished by making the owner a contract that re-enters during the call and observes/interferes with intermediate state).
